title: The Reclaimer
passages:
The ore stub smelled of cold iron and old brake dust. Rhea had the torch singing against the cradle bolts, blue-white sparks falling into the ballast between ties, while Teodoro held the work light steady with one hand and his tablet in the other, the screen washed out by the flare.

"Third bolt's seized," she said, not looking up. "Penetrant's been on it twenty minutes. If it snaps, we're drilling it out and that's an hour we don't have."

Teodoro tapped the manifest. "Manifest says the pod weighs four hundred twelve kilos. Cradle's rated for six. We cut it loose, the shop hoist takes the weight. No reason to rush the bolt."

"Reason is Ivo's filter alarm starts at oh-six-hundred. Reason is the water truck comes at oh-five-thirty and if the board's not clear, it turns around." She killed the torch, wiped her face with the back of a glove. "Give me the breaker bar."

He handed it over, and she set the jaw, braced a boot on the cradle flange, and leaned. Metal groaned. The bolt let go with a crack like a rifle shot.

"Two more," she said. "Then we roll the pod into the back bay and I can look at the diaphragm again before shift change."

A vibration came up through the rails, low and heavy, not the ghost trains' electric hum. Diesel, big-block, laboring up the grade. No transponder chirp cut the node's ambient chatter. No headlights swept the stub until the last ten meters, when twin beams snapped on and washed out the work light, the ties, Rhea's boots.

Teodoro shielded his tablet. "Service rig. Heavy. No ID broadcast."

The engine died. Air brakes hissed. A door clanged shut, and footsteps crunched ballast — slow, easy, like the man had nowhere urgent to be.

Rhea straightened, breaker bar resting on her shoulder. Teodoro stepped beside her, light lowered.

The man was lean, gray coveralls with the reclaimer's badge stitched dull on the chest: a stylized hook over a line. Late thirties, maybe. Hair cut short. Hands clean. He stopped three meters out, close enough to read the pod's stenciled numbers, far enough to keep his options open.

"Morning," he said. Voice pleasant, flat. "Who signs for ballast at Anza?"

Behind him, his rig's deck carried an empty cradle. Sized for exactly one box. The locking pins were already swung open.

Pell didn't smile. He reached into his coverall chest pocket and withdrew a stub of yellow brass, punched clean through with a node seal he didn't bother to hide. He walked past them to the relay counter — the steel desk bolted to the shop wall, screen dark until he woke it with a tap — and laid the token down like a bet.

"Warrant-token," he said. "Issued Kettering Central, 03:14 local. Derelict discrepancy, pod class, ballast designation. Node Anza is named."

Teodoro didn't hesitate. He set the work light on the counter, picked up the tablet, and read the token's code straight onto the board. His fingers moved the way they moved for shift logs: *manifest, confirm, enter.* The screen flickered. The board accepted it.

Then the board froze.

Shift slots grayed out one by one, names dimming to placeholder dashes. The resupply flag at the top corner flipped from GREEN to HOLD in a way that felt audible. The ambient chatter of the node — the low hum of scheduled rigs, the quiet tick of countdown timers — cut out.

Teodoro looked at the screen. His voice was flat, the same tone he used for shift changes. "Board's locked. No slot assignments. No resupply window. Water-and-parts truck at the north gate just got the hold signal."

Rhea's breaker bar dipped. "Ivo's spare scrubber cartridge is on that truck."

Teodoro nodded once. "Was. It's turning around now."

The inner door banged open. Nour stood there in her Shift 1 coveralls, clipboard in hand, the early light behind her making a silhouette of the broad shoulders and the set jaw. She looked at the board, then at Pell, then at Teodoro.

"My crew," she said. "Their names are gone. The whole day's wiped."

Rhea didn't look at Nour. She didn't look at the board. She turned, walked the five meters to the pod sitting on its cradle, and crouched beside the access panel she'd pried open hours ago. Her fingers found the repeater puck where she'd left it — palm-sized, matte black, held in by two zip ties she'd cut and replaced with a twist of safety wire. She popped the wire, pulled the puck free, and tapped its face.

The tiny screen lit. *36.4°C. LAST GOOD: 04:12.*

She stood, crossed to the counter, and held it out to Pell. "Repeater off the pod's databus. Keeps the last reading when the line goes dead. Thirty-six point four. Cargo doesn't run warm. He was breathing when he crossed the Blank."

Pell didn't turn his head. His eyes stayed on the frozen board, on the grayed-out shift slots and the HOLD flag blinking steady at the top corner. "Databus was cut. You said so yourself. The wire bundle that carries the rig's readings — severed. That puck held a number because the repeater's job is to hold the last good number. It doesn't know the line went dead. It doesn't know the box went cold."

"He was alive at oh-four-twelve."

"He was a reading at oh-four-twelve. A reading isn't a witness. A number isn't a life." Pell finally looked at her, and his face was calm, almost kind. "The warrant names ballast. The manifest names ballast. The node's own plate names ballast. You want to argue temperature, you're arguing with a ghost."

He didn't take the puck. Rhea's hand stayed extended, the little black screen glowing 36.4 in the shop's dim light. Behind her, Nour set her clipboard down on a workbench with a careful, deliberate clack. Teodoro's tablet screen reflected the same frozen board.

"Then we argue with the plate," Rhea said. "Teodoro. Read it."

Pell turned to the relay operator. "Teodoro. As relay operator. Confirm the cargo on this node's manifest plate."

Teodoro didn't look at Pell. He didn't look at Rhea, or Nour, or the frozen board. His eyes went to the manifest plate riveted to the shop wall above the counter — a steel rectangle stamped with Anza's node code, its fields waiting for a stylus or a fingertip to wake them. He knew every line of it. He'd written most of them.

He tapped the plate's edge. The screen warmed, white text on black.

"Bay four," he said. The voice was the one he used at shift change, the one that carried through the yard when the wind was wrong. "Shift two. Discharge logged twenty-one forty-seven, Kettering local. Weight entered: four hundred twelve kilos. Designation: ballast. Seal authority: V. Ospina, stamp number seven-zero-nine. Receiving node: Anza. Received: zero-four-twelve local, ore stub, unmanned siding. Condition: sealed, no exceptions noted."

He stopped. The plate had no more lines.

"Operator confirmation," Pell said. Not a question. "Teodoro. You confirm this cargo as ballast."

Teodoro's fingers hovered over the plate. The stylus in his hand didn't move. "The plate says ballast. The weight says ballast. The seal says ballast. I confirm what the plate says."

"Then the warrant stands," Pell said. "The node holds ballast. The node surrenders ballast. The board stays frozen until the cradle's loaded and the rig clears the stub."

Rhea's jaw tightened. She still held the repeater puck, its screen dimming now to save power. "He was breathing at oh-four-twelve. The plate doesn't change that."

"The plate is what the line reads," Pell said. "The line doesn't read breath. The line reads weight, seal, designation. You want the line to read different, you change the plate. You don't change the plate with a temperature reading from a cut bus."

Nour shifted at the workbench. Her clipboard stayed where she'd set it. "The water truck has Ivo's filter. The resupply has the scrubber cartridges for Shift three. The parts crate has the bearing races for the north gate winch. All of it on HOLD because the plate says ballast."

Teodoro looked at her. "The plate says what was entered. I entered what was given. Bay four, shift two, twenty-one forty-seven, four-twelve kilos, ballast." He recited it again, quieter. "That's the confirmation."

"Then we're done here," Pell said. He turned toward the pod, toward the empty cradle on his rig's deck. "Load it. The clock's running."

The inner door hadn't opened. The shop's air was still, the kind of stillness that settles after a blast goes off and before the dust hits the floor. In that stillness, a sound rose from the back bay — a wheeze, a click, a wheeze, a click. Rhythmic. Mechanical. The disc of heavy glove rubber patching Ivo's respirator diaphragm, flexing with each breath he took in his sleep.

Teodoro's stylus touched the plate. *Confirmed,* the screen flashed. *Ballast. No exceptions.*

The wheeze-click continued. Four hundred twelve kilos of ballast, breathing in the back bay.

The inner door swung inward on hinges that didn't squeak. The man stood framed in it, left shoulder strapped tight to his chest with a triangular bandage knotted over clean gray coveralls — Kettering issue, Bay 4 patch still visible on the sleeve. His right hand hovered at the strap's edge, fingers brushing the knot like he'd tied it himself and wasn't sure he trusted the work. His face was pale, scraped along the jawline, eyes moving in the shop's dim light: Pell at the counter, Teodoro frozen over the plate, Nour at the bench, Rhea with the dimming puck still in her outstretched hand. Ivo's wheeze-click rose from the back bay, steady as a metronome.

The man's throat worked. "What's ballast?"

Teodoro didn't glance at Pell. He didn't look at Rhea or Nour. His gaze settled on the man's face, direct and unhurried, the same way he read a manifest to a tired crew at shift change. "Ballast is weight you carry so the line stays balanced. Cheap weight. Dirt, scrap, water tanks, whatever the schedule says goes in the box so the paying cargo rides smooth. You get logged as weight. You get sealed. You get delivered. The node that receives you signs for weight. That's all."

The man's eyes flicked to the manifest plate, still glowing on the wall. *Bay four. Shift two. Discharge logged twenty-one forty-seven. Weight entered: four hundred twelve kilos. Designation: ballast.*

Ivo's voice came through the mask from the back bay, thin but clear, each word timed between wheezes. "Ballast is the cheap stuff. You carry it so the expensive stuff don't shift. Nobody asks the dirt what it thinks. Dirt just rides."

The man took a step into the shop. His boot struck the concrete flat, no limp. He stopped at the counter's edge, close enough to touch the frozen board's grayed slots. His gaze dropped to the repeater puck in Rhea's hand, its screen dark now, then back to the plate.

"Four-twelve kilos," he said. His voice was rough, unused. "That's what it says."

"Four-twelve," Teodoro confirmed. "Logged at Kettering. Received at Anza zero-four-twelve. Sealed, no exceptions."

The man's hand left his strap. He braced both palms on the counter's steel top, leaning forward like he was reading a schedule he'd memorized years ago. "I was at Kettering at twenty-one-forty-seven. Bay four. Shift two. I remember the foreman yelling about the seal stamp sticking. I remember the lid coming down. I remember counting backward from ten in a voice that wasn't mine." He paused. His eyes found Pell, then Rhea, then Teodoro again. "I'm not missing. I'm already filed."

Pell didn't flinch. He didn't look at the man like he'd just grown a second head. He looked at him like a manifest line that had finally resolved itself — inconvenient, but resolved.

"Good," Pell said. "Then you know the drill." He turned to his rig, slate in hand, and started walking toward the empty cradle on the deck. His boots didn't hurry. "Load the box. Clear the stub. Board unlocks, resupply rolls, everybody eats."

Rhea moved before he took three steps. She didn't run — she never ran — but the tool cart on its casters shrieked across the concrete, and she planted it square between Pell and the pod's cradle, the breaker bar still hooked over her shoulder like a rifle. "Box stays. He stays."

Pell stopped. He glanced at the cart, at the wrenches and the hydraulic jack and the coil of safety wire spilling over the edge, then at Rhea. "Mechanic. You're not on the warrant."

"I'm on the node," she said. "And the node's got a respirator alarm fixing to scream in the back bay. You want the board unfrozen? You wait until Ivo's got a filter that doesn't whistle."

Nour stepped up beside the cart, arms crossed, clipboard forgotten. Her voice carried the yard. "Anza eats through winter on the line's good schedule. One stranger — one *breathing* stranger — isn't worth a node's shifts. You hand him over, the water truck comes back, the scrubber cartridges come back, the bearing races come back. My crew gets their names back on the board. We keep our place on the line. That's the math."

Pell looked from Rhea to Nour to Teodoro, who stood frozen over the manifest plate, stylus still in hand. He looked at the man leaning on the counter, shoulder strapped, eyes bright and hard. Then he looked at the back bay door, where the wheeze-click had stopped.

Three short tones pierced the shop. *Beep. Beep. Beep.*

Ivo's respirator. Filter alarm. Three tones meant the cartridge was at end-of-life, and the spare was on the truck that had just turned around at the north gate.

Pell's head tilted, the only sign he'd heard. He raised his slate, stylus scratching. "Handover by the oh-six-hundred shift change. That's twenty minutes. If the cradle's not loaded and the rig not clearing the stub by then, the freeze holds through the next resupply cycle. Water, parts, filters — all of it. You'll run the node on what's in the lockers until the line decides Anza's worth another window."

He capped his stylus, slammed the slate shut. "Your clock's running. I'll be at the north gate with a second signature." He turned, walked back to his rig, and climbed into the cab without a backward glance.

The diesel coughed to life. Air brakes released with a sigh.

Rhea didn't move the cart. Her knuckles were white on the breaker bar. "Twenty minutes."

Nour's jaw worked. "Fifteen to the north gate if the service rig takes the haul road. Five to argue with a reclaimer who's already signed twice."

Teodoro set the stylus down on the plate. *Confirmed. Ballast. No exceptions.* The words glowed on the steel. "The board doesn't unlock until the warrant's satisfied. Pell's signature, node's surrender. That's the rule."

The man pushed off the counter. His good hand found the strap knot again. "Then the rule needs a witness who isn't a number."

In the back bay, the respirator wheezed again. Three more tones. *Beep. Beep. Beep.*

The man didn't wait for permission. He pushed off the counter, shoulder strapped, bootfall even on the concrete, and walked through the shop door into the yard. Cold air hit him — thin, dry, smelling of diesel and ore dust — and he didn't flinch. Just kept moving until he stood in the open space between the shop bay and Pell's idling rig, the empty cradle on its deck gaping like a mouth.

Rhea followed him out. Nour came after, Teodoro a step behind, the manifest plate's glow spilling from the doorway at their backs. Ivo's respirator wheezed and clicked in the back bay, three tones, three tones, a clock nobody could stop.

The man turned. Faced them all — Pell in the cab above, Rhea at his left, Nour at his right, Teodoro holding the door. His good hand came up, palm out, the gesture slow and deliberate.

"No cradle," he said. "No box. No weight entry on a plate that says ballast." His voice carried across the stub, rough but steady. "You want me on the board, put me on the board. Name. Bunk. Shift. Something that counts. I'll sign it myself."

Pell's cab door didn't open. The diesel rumbled, steady. From the window, a slate appeared, stylus scratching in the cab's dome light. Pell's voice came through the glass, calm as a shift log. "Refusal noted. Node Anza, 05:42 local. Cargo — " He paused. " — *declares living witness status*. Countersign required. Second signature at north gate, 06:00 shift change. Warrant holds until then."

The stylus capped. The slate vanished. Pell's face appeared in the window, pale in the dome light, and he looked down at the man standing in the cold.

"Twenty minutes," Pell said. "I'll be back with the second name. You find a countersign, the board unlocks. You don't, the freeze rides through resupply." The engine note deepened as he shifted into gear. "Clock's yours."

The rig moved. Air brakes hissed. The cradle's empty pins caught the light as it rolled past, turning toward the haul road, the north gate, the open line.

Rhea didn't watch it go. She looked at the man — really looked, the way she'd look at a cracked weld or a seized bolt, seeing the thing whole. Her breaker bar slid from her shoulder to hang at her side, forgotten.

"Name," she said. "You got one?"

The man's jaw worked. His eyes moved across their faces — Nour's arms still crossed, Teodoro's tablet dark in his hand, Rhea's grease-stained gloves, the shop door framing Ivo's wheeze-click. Memory flickered behind his eyes, pieces clicking into place like couplers locking.

"Marlowe," he said. "Decklan Marlowe. Bay four, shift two, Kettering. Loader. Discharged twenty-one forty-seven." He took a breath, the cold burning his lungs. "I remember the foreman. I remember the lid. I remember the second pair of hands that held it while the stamp came down."

Rhea's mouth twisted, something between a grin and a grimace. "Decklan Marlowe. Bay four. Shift two. Loader." She said it like she was torquing a spec bolt. "Node Anza, 05:43. Witness entered. Mechanic's authority — " She tapped her badge. " — Rhea, relay mechanic. Badge four-one-one. He's not ballast. He's crew."

Nour exhaled, long and sharp. "Mechanic's authority doesn't unlock a reclaimer's warrant. You need a seal authority. Bay four, shift two — that's Ospina's stamp. Ospina's at Kettering."

"Then Ospina gets here," Rhea said. "Or we find another seal. Twenty minutes, Nour. Fifteen to the north gate. Five to make a call."

Teodoro's tablet woke in his hand. His fingers moved. "I can raise Kettering dispatch. Channel's open if the board's not fully locked — just the shift slots. Comms still run." He paused, stylus hovering. "But the resupply hold is line-level. Only a seal authority countersign clears a reclamation warrant. That's the rule."

"Rules change," the man — Marlowe — said. His hand found his strap knot again. "When someone stands up and says them different."

Down the stub, past the ore bins where shadows pooled deep, a set of headlights snapped on. No transponder chirp. No ID broadcast. Just twin beams cutting the dark, coming fast on the haul road from the north gate direction — *toward* them, not away.

Rhea's breaker bar came up. Nour's hand went to the radio at her belt. Teodoro's stylus froze over the screen.

The rig crested the rise. Service rig, heavy, unmarked. Coming in hot.
